title: Privacy Games
extended_summary:
This paper studies how privacy concerns change strategic behavior in a simple Bayesian signaling game. The authors ask whether the behavior of a self-interested, utility-maximizing agent with explicit privacy costs can be modeled using differential privacy ideas, and how that behavior differs depending on how privacy loss is operationalized. The central question is not about educational technology or AI, but about the game-theoretic behavior of agents when one player tries to infer another player’s hidden type.

The paper introduces a family of “coupon games” in which agent B has a secret binary type and sends a signal to agent A, who then takes an action and/or makes a prediction. The authors analyze three payment structures: symmetric proper scoring rules, identity-matrix payments, and a variant with an opt-out option. For each game they derive Bayesian Nash equilibria and compare them to a benchmark game without signaling. The analysis is theoretical and mathematical, with no human participants, experiments, schools, teachers, or instructional setting.

The main conclusion is that small changes in how privacy costs are modeled can lead to very different equilibrium behavior. In some settings B randomizes in a way related to randomized response; in others at least one type behaves deterministically; and in some parameter regimes the receiver’s posterior becomes symmetric or otherwise threshold-based. The paper also shows that whether an information-disclosure game is worthwhile for the receiver depends on the payment rule and parameter values, but it does not address education, coaching, lesson feedback, or generative AI use.
